questions.prompt: Choose the correct main clause: "If you press this button, the lift ___."

options.text: will starting
started
will to start
will start

questions.explanation: The main clause of a first conditional takes will + base verb: the lift will start. "will starting" and "will to start" change the verb after will, which must stay bare; "started" is the simple past and says nothing about the result to come.

options.text: If the train goes faster, we'll be on time.
If it is sunny, we will go to the beach.
If he doesn't come, I will call him.
If Dad will have time, he will drive us.

questions.explanation: "If Dad will have time, he will drive us." is wrong: will never goes in the if clause — it should be "If Dad has time". The three other sentences follow the pattern: simple present in the if clause (goes, is, doesn't come) and will in the result.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a correct first conditional?

options.text: If it will rain, we stay inside.
If it rained, we will stay inside.
If it rains, we will stay inside.
If it rains, we will stayed inside.

questions.explanation: "If it rains, we will stay inside." — simple present (rains) in the if clause, will + base verb (will stay) in the result. "If it will rain" puts will in the wrong clause; "rained" is the simple past; "will stayed" puts a past form after will.

questions.prompt: Complete both blanks: "If she ___ the exam, her parents ___ very proud."

options.text: will pass ... are
passes ... will be
passed ... will be
pass ... will be

questions.explanation: "passes ... will be": the if clause takes the simple present with -s for she (passes), the main clause takes will + be. "will pass ... are" swaps the two tenses; "passed" is the simple past; "pass" forgets the -s of she.

questions.prompt: Read: "If the weather is fine, we will visit the old medina." What does the speaker mean?

options.text: They will visit the medina whatever the weather.
They visited the medina because it was fine.
Fine weather is the condition for the visit.
The visit is the condition for fine weather.

questions.explanation: Fine weather is the condition for the visit: the if clause (the weather is fine) states the condition, the main clause (we will visit) the result. The visit is not sure "whatever the weather", it has not already happened, and it is not the condition — the clause with if is.

questions.prompt: Combine into one first-conditional sentence: "Perhaps the train is late. Then I will miss my meeting."

options.text: If the train will be late, I miss my meeting.
If the train is late, I will miss my meeting.
If the train is late I will miss, my meeting.
If the train was late, I will miss my meeting.

questions.explanation: "If the train is late, I will miss my meeting." — the possible event becomes the if clause in the simple present, the consequence takes will, and a comma closes the if clause. The other versions put will in the if clause, place the comma inside the result, or use the simple past "was".
